issues.legal_issue: A subsisting mining lease continues after an estate vests in the State, with the State substituted as lessor and the leaseholder's title under the lease preserved.
material_facts: The Court proceeded on the assumption that the original mining lease was valid and subsisting when the estate vested in the State.
The lease covered mines and minerals within the estate.
issues.conclusion: The vesting statute created a statutory lease in favour of the existing leaseholders for the remainder of the original lease term, on the original terms and conditions, and did not extinguish their title under the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(1) and (2) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 provides that a subsisting lease of mines and minerals is deemed, from the date of vesting, to be a lease by the State to the existing leaseholder for the remainder of the term, on the same terms and conditions. Bihar Mines Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1967 SC 887, explains that this creates a new statutory lease on vesting and does not put an end to the leaseholder's title.

predicates.mining_lease_subsisted_at_estate_vesting: A leaseholder held a subsisting lease of mines or minerals when the estate containing them vested in the State.

issues.definition: When a mining lease was subsisting at the vesting of the estate, the existing leaseholder continues as a lessee under the State.

issues.legal_issue: A mining-leases controller cannot terminate a statutory lease created when an estate vests in the State by relying on an order modifying the earlier lease.
material_facts: The original mining lease was subsisting when the estate vested in the State, and the Court held that the vesting statute created a new statutory lease.
The Controller of Mining Leases purported to modify the original lease and make it terminable before its original term expired.
issues.conclusion: The Controller had no authority in law to terminate the lease, and the purported termination was invalid and without legal effect.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 creates a new statutory lease on vesting. Following Bihar Mines Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1967 SC 887, the Court held that the Controller's order under Rule 6 of the Mining Lease (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956 could not terminate that lease.

predicates.mining_lease_became_state_lease_on_vesti: An existing mining lease became a lease under the State when the estate vested in the State.
predicates.controller_purported_to_terminate_lease: A mining-leases controller issued an order purporting to end that lease before its term expired.

issues.definition: If an existing mining lease became a State lease on vesting and a controller purported to terminate it, the controller lacked authority to do so.

issues.legal_issue: Entries in revenue and mutation registers are not conclusive proof of proprietary title.
material_facts: The leaseholders relied on entries in Register D to show that their predecessor was proprietor of the estate and could grant the original mining lease.
The entries reflected changes recorded in the land registers, and the leaseholders did not produce clear, conclusive and unimpeachable documentary evidence establishing the predecessor's title.
issues.conclusion: The Register D entries were strong prima facie evidence but were not conclusive evidence of title.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Land Registration Act, 1876, Register D records changes affecting entries in other registers. Nirman Singh v. Lal Rudra Partab Narain Singh, 53 IA 220, holds that mutation proceedings are fiscal enquiries and do not determine title. Sri Marudeswarar Temple v. Dhanalakshmi Ammal, Civil Appeal No. 236 of 1961, holds that a revenue entry is not conclusive of title. The Court also referred to Lodna Colliery Company (1920) Ltd. v. Bhola Nath Roy, AIR 1964 SC 918, concerning proprietary rights in sub-soil minerals.

predicates.title_claim_rests_on_revenue_register_en: A party relies on entries in a revenue or mutation register to establish proprietary title.

issues.definition: When a title claim rests on revenue-register entries, those entries do not conclusively establish title.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional writ is not an appropriate means to resolve a serious dispute over title and displace a person in possession when the claimant lacks clear and conclusive proof of title.
material_facts: The party opposing the writ was in possession under a mining lease granted by the State and had carried on prospecting operations.
The writ applicants were not in possession and sought orders that would disturb the existing possession.

The opposing party seriously disputed the title on which the writ applicants relied, and the applicants had not produced clear, conclusive and unimpeachable documentary evidence establishing that title.
The writ applicants' earlier possession and their prima facie title were not treated as a final determination of title.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition was not competent in these circumstances; the title dispute was left open for determination in a suitably framed civil suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, writ proceedings are not appropriate where serious factual disputes and a contested title would have to be resolved to grant relief that displaces the person in possession. Sohan Lal v. Union of India, [1957] SCR 738, states that a title suit is the proper remedy in such circumstances and that writ relief may be available where the facts are undisputed and title is clear. Mohd. Hanif v. State of Assam, [1969] 2 SCC 782, was distinguished because it concerned executive interference with the petitioner's own possession.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_challenging_property_grant and serious_title_dispute and respondent_in_possession and relief_requires_displacing_possession and not clear_conclusive_title_evidence

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_property: A claimant brings a constitutional writ petition challenging a grant affecting property.
predicates.serious_title_dispute: The parties seriously dispute the claimant's title to the property.
predicates.respondent_in_possession: The person opposing the claim is in possession of the property.
predicates.relief_requires_displacing_possession: The relief sought would require the court to displace the person in possession.
predicates.clear_conclusive_title_evidence: The claimant has produced clear and conclusive evidence establishing title.

issues.definition: When a writ challenges a property grant, title is seriously disputed, the opposing party is in possession, relief would displace that party, and clear title evidence is absent, the writ is not an appropriate means to displace the possessor.
